intro: Five routes, same principle: learn a little, make something small, then check your understanding. Start at the level that matches what you can already do—not the level you think you should be.

paths.title: Understand AI without the jargon
paths.subtitle: A calm on-ramp for curious adults who want to use AI thoughtfully and explain it clearly.
paths.certificates: One free Google badge and one free Kaggle certificate are available in this route.
paths.bestFor: Nurses, writers, small-business owners, parents, and anyone who keeps hearing AI terms they are too polite to ask about.
paths.prereqs: None. No math, no coding, no prerequisite course.
paths.summary: Build a working vocabulary, practice a repeatable prompt loop, and develop the judgment to notice when AI is helpful, wrong, or inappropriate.

steps.title: Get the big picture
steps.description: Start with a 45-minute explanation and a friendly university course. The goal is not to memorize terms; it is to replace vague anxiety with a few accurate sentences.

steps.title: Learn how machines learn
steps.description: Skim Google's ML fundamentals and watch one visual explanation. You are building a mental model of training, prediction, and error—not becoming an engineer in a weekend.

steps.title: Practice a real prompt
steps.description: Take a short prompting course, then use Google's whitepaper to understand why one prompt works better than another. Test everything on a low-stakes, non-sensitive task.

steps.title: Build your judgment
steps.description: Use an ethics course and a human-centered design guide to make your own rules for privacy, verification, disclosure, and when to stop and ask a person.

project.title: A one-page AI field note
project.description: Write a plain-English explanation of generative AI in five paragraphs, include a prompt template you tested, and finish with five personal rules for safe use.
project.proof: A document you could hand to a colleague. Bonus: record a five-minute voice note explaining it without jargon.

paths.after: Move to the Python and data foundations route if you want to make tools yourself, or stay here and deepen your practice with the 30/60/90-day plan.

paths.title: Python and data, without the bootcamp
paths.subtitle: A practical foundation for people who want to clean data, train a first model, and know when the result is believable.
paths.certificates: Kaggle certificates are free and quick; freeCodeCamp certifications are free but long.
paths.bestFor: Anyone willing to practice a little code each week. Useful for authors tracking sales, small businesses studying demand, or healthcare workers learning with public data.
paths.prereqs: Comfort using a browser and editing a spreadsheet. No prior programming required, but consistency is.
paths.summary: Learn just enough Python to be dangerous, get comfortable with tabular data, build a first model, and tell an honest story about what it can and cannot prove.

steps.title: Python on-ramp
steps.description: Use Kaggle's short in-browser course as the required spine. Keep freeCodeCamp's larger certification in reserve for when you want a long, project-based credential.

steps.title: Make data less scary
steps.description: Learn pandas through small exercises, then use freeCodeCamp's data-analysis curriculum for deeper project practice. Pick a public dataset you actually find interesting.

steps.title: Train a first model
steps.description: Build a decision tree and random forest in Kaggle, then use Google's crash course to understand what the model is optimizing and where it can fail.

steps.title: Get honest about evaluation
steps.description: Learn about validation, missing data, and pipelines. Read Machine Learning Yearning for the project-level judgment that code tutorials often skip.

steps.title: Make a portfolio project
steps.description: Only after the smaller pieces feel familiar, choose a long freeCodeCamp certification or go deeper into neural networks with Kaggle. Use the other as optional follow-up.

project.title: One honest data story
project.description: Choose a public, non-sensitive dataset. Ask one clear question, establish a baseline, train a simple model, and report one meaningful limit alongside your result.
project.proof: A clean notebook and a one-page README with the question, data source, method, metric, and 'what this does not prove'.

paths.after: You are ready for the builder route: LLM applications, agents, and MCP. Or continue into deep learning for a more mathematical route.

paths.title: Build with LLMs, agents, and MCP
paths.subtitle: From a first API call to a small agent that uses tools—with free certificates available along the way.
paths.certificates: Hugging Face offers free Agents and MCP certificates. DeepLearning.AI lessons are free; its certificates require PRO.
paths.bestFor: People who can already write a little Python and want to build useful, local-first tools rather than only chat with a model.
paths.prereqs: Basic Python (variables, functions, lists, a little file handling), comfort with the command line, and patience with error messages.
paths.summary: Learn how LLM applications are put together, how agents use tools, and how MCP connects models to outside data. Each stage ends with something small you can run.

steps.title: Python and API confidence
steps.description: Fill the coding gaps with DeepLearning.AI's beginner Python course. Skim Microsoft's Generative AI curriculum for the app-building vocabulary, not as a race.

steps.title: Understand the model layer
steps.description: Work through the first chapters of the Hugging Face LLM course. Focus on tokens, transformers, datasets, and evaluation before trying to fine-tune anything.

steps.title: Prompt, call, and constrain
steps.description: Use DeepLearning.AI's prompting short course to turn a fuzzy idea into instructions, then enforce a format in code. Keep API keys in environment variables, never in your repo.

steps.title: Build your first agent loop
steps.description: Learn the goal → tool → observation → stop loop. Take Hugging Face's Agents course for structured practice, with Microsoft's AI Agents curriculum as a second perspective.

steps.title: Connect tools safely with MCP
steps.description: Build an MCP mental model with the Hugging Face course, then use Microsoft's curriculum and the official docs when you need implementation detail. Start read-only, with explicit permissions.

steps.title: Ship a small capstone
steps.description: Use the Kaggle/Google agent intensive for structure and community, or design your own project. The finish line is a tested tool with a README—not a folder of half-finished demos.

project.title: A small tool with a tool-use boundary
project.description: Build one narrow agent or MCP-connected app: a reading-log helper, a public-data lookup, or a local document Q&A tool. Use synthetic or public data, require confirmation before any write action, and document what it cannot do.
project.proof: A public repo or local project with setup steps, a demo, a privacy note, and evidence that it runs from a clean start.

paths.after: Go deeper into evaluation, observability, and security. Or use the finished project as the foundation for an ASDALE DYNAMICS template or small product.

paths.title: Free AI coding and local models
paths.subtitle: A practical toolkit for GitHub, an AI coding partner, and private models that run on your own machine.
paths.certificates: Hugging Face's MCP certificate is free. GitHub's optional certification exam is paid; Copilot and Ollama do not issue certificates.
paths.bestFor: Writers, small-business owners, and early builders who want a public code workspace, an AI coding assistant, and a model that runs locally.
paths.prereqs: Comfort with a browser and basic file navigation. No prior programming is required for the GitHub step; later steps assume a little Python or willingness to follow setup instructions.
paths.summary: Set up GitHub, learn to use Copilot as a careful pair, run an open model locally with Ollama, connect a tool through MCP, and finish one small local-first project you can explain.

steps.title: Make GitHub your workshop
steps.description: Work through GitHub Foundations Part 1. Learn repositories, commits, branches, pull requests, Projects, and Markdown. Publish a small README as your first artifact—not a perfect portfolio.

steps.title: Pair with an AI coding assistant
steps.description: Use GitHub Copilot Fundamentals to learn what the assistant is good at, where it is confidently wrong, and how prompt context changes the result. Keep reviewing every suggestion before accepting it.

steps.title: Run a model on your own machine
steps.description: Follow Ollama's official quickstart: install it, pull a small open model, and make one local request. Test a task with fabricated or public data, and note the memory and speed limits you observe.

steps.title: Connect a tool with MCP
steps.description: Learn the MCP mental model with Hugging Face's free course, then use Microsoft's curriculum for implementation detail. Start read-only and give the tool the narrowest permissions that still work.

steps.title: Ship a local-first capstone
steps.description: Use Microsoft's Generative AI curriculum and Hugging Face's Agents course as references, then build one narrow helper. Keep prompts and files on your machine, require confirmation before writes, and document what the tool cannot do.

project.title: A private local-first helper
project.description: Build a small note organizer, document Q&A tool, or reading-log helper that runs against a local Ollama model. Use synthetic or public text, keep secrets out of the repo, and add one read-only MCP tool if the project calls for it.
project.proof: A GitHub repository with setup steps, a short demo, a privacy note, two failure cases, and evidence that it runs from a clean start without paid API keys.

paths.after: Add tests and an evaluation checklist, or turn the project into a reusable template. If you want deeper model work, move into Python and data or the deep-learning route.

paths.title: Deep learning, from first principles
paths.subtitle: A slower, more rigorous route for people who want to understand the machinery, not only use the API.
paths.certificates: Kaggle's Intro to Deep Learning certificate is free. The most valuable output here is a reproducible project and model card.
paths.bestFor: Builders who have finished a first ML project and now want the math, model internals, and research habits behind modern deep learning.
paths.prereqs: Comfortable Python, basic calculus and linear algebra, and at least one machine-learning course or equivalent project experience.
paths.summary: Use code-first courses to keep momentum, open textbooks to fill the math, and primary lectures to see how the field reasons. Expect to loop back, not master everything in one pass.

steps.title: Refresh the math you need
steps.description: Use selected chapters of Mathematics for Machine Learning and visual videos. Aim for intuition about vectors, gradients, and probability—not exam perfection.

steps.title: Build first
steps.description: Take fast.ai's code-first course alongside its free book. Train models, break things, and develop a feel for learning rates, overfitting, and data quality before diving into proofs.

steps.title: Connect theory to implementation
steps.description: Read and run Dive into Deep Learning, then complete Kaggle's short deep-learning course as a checkpoint. Rewrite at least one model from scratch in a small notebook.

steps.title: Learn from primary lectures
steps.description: Watch MIT 6.S191 and selected Andrej Karpathy lectures. Take notes as if you will explain each idea to a smart colleague who has never trained a model.

steps.title: Read the reference shelf
steps.description: Use Deep Learning as a reference when a concept will not click, and An Introduction to Statistical Learning to keep classical machine learning in view. You are not required to read every page.

steps.title: Fine-tune and document
steps.description: Use the Hugging Face LLM course for a guided fine-tuning or evaluation project, then write a model card with intended use, limits, data provenance, and failure cases.

project.title: A reproducible model study
project.description: Choose a public dataset or small open model. Establish a baseline, test one clear hypothesis, document the compute budget, evaluate beyond a single score, and state who should not rely on it.
project.proof: A reproducible repository, training log, evaluation table, and a model card written for a non-expert reader.

paths.after: Specialize in evaluation, interpretability, efficient fine-tuning, or safety—and keep a small project shipping while you read.
